title: 2023 Trends: A Report on Accounting Education, the CPA Exam and Public Accounting Firms' Hiring of Recent Graduates
pub: AICPA & CIMA (Association of International Certified Professional Accountants)
author: AICPA & CIMA

dom.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction

mo.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

kp.d: The article reports findings from the AICPA's biennial 2023 Trends report: 47,067 students earned accounting bachelor's degrees in 2021-22, down 7.8%, while accounting master's degrees fell 6.4% to 18,238. Comparative declines in the previous report were 2.8% and 8.4%, respectively. These are accounting workforce-pipeline findings, not claims about AI or legal services.
qs: Some 47,067 students earned a bachelor’s degree in accounting in the 2021-22 school year, down 7.8% from the previous year, according to 2023 Trends: A Report on Accounting Education, the CPA Exam and Public Accounting Firms’ Hiring of Recent Graduates.
The number of students who earned a master’s degree in accounting, meanwhile, fell 6.4% to 18,238. In the previous Trends report, the comparative rates of decline were 2.8% and 8.4%, respectively.

kp.k: Enrollment expectations improved, but remained projections
kp.d: Three-quarters of responding bachelor's programs and 78% of responding master's programs expected 2023-24 enrollment to equal or exceed 2021-22 levels, compared with 58% for both categories in the previous report. These expectations concern responding programs and do not establish an actual enrollment recovery.
qs: Three-quarters of responding university bachelor’s programs and 78% of responding master’s programs expect enrollment in 2023-24 to be the same or higher as in 2021-22.
That compares to 58% for both program categories in the previous Trends report.

kp.k: AICPA contextualizes shortages within broader university contraction
kp.d: Jan Taylor, the AICPA's academic in residence, describes accounting graduates as continuing on a downward trajectory while noting that overall U.S. university enrollment and earned degrees also contracted during the period. Taylor reports increased profession-wide mobilization and coordination on talent-shortage solutions over the preceding year, without attributing the decline to AI.
qs: “We’re still on a downward trajectory for accounting graduates, although it’s worthwhile to note U.S. university enrollment and earned degrees collectively shrank during this period,” said Jan Taylor, the AICPA’s academic in residence.
“The AICPA remains focused on advocating profession-wide solutions to the talent shortage, and we saw increased mobilization and coordination in these efforts over the past year.”

kp.k: Insufficient firm responses prevented valid graduate-hiring estimates
kp.d: Although Trends has measured accounting graduate supply and demand since 1971, the accounting-firm response rate for this edition was too low for statistical validity despite an extended survey period. The AICPA therefore could not accurately project public-accounting graduate hires for 2021 and was investigating survey timing, delivery methods and promotion to improve subsequent data collection.
qs: The Trends report has been published since 1971, measuring both the supply of and demand for accounting graduates.

This year, however, the response rate from accounting firms on their hiring practices was too low to be statistically valid – despite an extension of the time the survey was in the field – so the AICPA is unable to accurately project the number of graduates hired into public accounting in 2021.
The organization is looking into a number of issues, including the survey’s timing, delivery methods and promotion, to ensure more complete data in the next report.

kp.k: Graduate demographic composition remained largely stable
kp.d: The report describes gender and racial-ethnic composition as similar to the previous edition, except that Hispanic/Latino graduates increased by almost a percentage point and nonresident alien graduates decreased by a similar amount in both 2020-21 and 2021-22.
qs: The gender ratio and racial-ethnic mix of accounting graduates remained similar to the previous Trends report, with two exceptions: Hispanic/Latino graduates increased by almost a percentage point and nonresident alien graduates decreased by a similar amount in both the 2020-21 and 2021-22 academic years.

kp.k: Private institutions experienced larger master's degree declines
kp.d: Accounting master's degrees earned at private institutions fell 10.9% in 2021-22, compared with a 3.3% decline at public institutions. The article reports this institutional difference without providing a causal explanation.
qs: Master’s degrees earned at private institutions fell 10.9% in the 2021-22 school year, while those earned at public schools decreased 3.3%.

kp.k: Responding firms anticipated stable or increased staffing
kp.d: Among responding firms, 91% expected to hire the same or more new accounting graduates in the next year, and 60% expected the same or more CPAs on staff in 2023 compared with 2022. These are respondents' expectations, not observed hiring outcomes or statistically valid industry-wide estimates, given the report's stated response-rate limitation.
qs: For accounting firms who responded to the survey, hiring expectations are optimistic for new hires of accounting graduates, with 91% of respondents saying they expect to hire the same or more new graduates in the next year.
Sixty percent of surveyed firms reported they expect to have the same or higher number of CPAs on staff in 2023 compared to 2022.

kp.k: CPA candidates declined; exam activity rose before licensure changes
kp.d: Unique CPA Exam candidates fell from 72,271 in 2021 to 67,335 in 2022. The article separately reports rising exam sections taken in 2023, attributing this partly to candidates seeking completion before CPA Evolution began in 2024. That licensure model combines core accounting, auditing, tax and technology competencies with deeper expertise in one of three disciplines; the reported increase in sections is not presented as an increase in unique candidates.
qs: The number of unique CPA Exam candidates declined from 72,271 in 2021 to 67,335 in 2022.

The number of exam sections taken in 2023 is on the upswing, in part because test takers are looking to complete their requirements before the 2024 onset of CPA Evolution, a new licensure model that focuses on building core competencies in accounting, auditing, tax, and technology while developing deeper expertise in one of three disciplines: information systems and controls; tax compliance and planning; or business analysis and reporting.

kp.k: AICPA organized coordinated responses to pipeline shortages
kp.d: The AICPA convened the multi-stakeholder National Pipeline Advisory Group to explore data-driven responses to the talent shortage, with a draft national strategy expected at its governing Council meeting in May 2024. It was also advancing a Pipeline Acceleration Plan comprising initiatives described as already having considerable professional consensus. The article reports initiatives and a planned deliverable, not demonstrated effects on talent supply.
qs: a multi-stakeholder group that is exploring data-driven approaches to address the talent shortage.
The advisory group is expected to deliver a draft national strategy plan at the AICPA’s governing Council meeting in May 2024.
a series of initiatives that already have considerable consensus within the profession.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: This cross-domain source reports a shrinking accounting talent pipeline alongside respondents’ relatively optimistic enrollment and hiring expectations. It makes no claim about AI causing these changes.
pts.d: The AICPA news release summarizing its 2023 Trends report states that accounting bachelor’s degrees fell 7.8% to 47,067 and master’s degrees fell 6.4% to 18,238 in 2021–22. Unique CPA Exam candidates declined from 72,271 in 2021 to 67,335 in 2022. Despite those declines, 75% of responding bachelor’s programs and 78% of responding master’s programs expected stable or higher enrollment in 2023–24 relative to 2021–22. Among responding accounting firms, 91% expected to hire the same or more new accounting graduates in the next year, and 60% expected stable or higher CPA staffing in 2023 relative to 2022. The source also reports rising exam-section activity in 2023, partly attributed to candidates seeking to finish before the new CPA Evolution licensure model begins. These are accounting-domain findings and expectations, not evidence of AI-driven displacement or changes to legal services.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on figures and survey responses summarized from the AICPA’s biennial Trends report, with an explicit warning that firm responses cannot support a statistically valid hiring projection.
pts.d: Degree and CPA Exam counts are reported as historical findings; enrollment and hiring expectations are respondents’ forecasts rather than observed outcomes. The supplied release does not provide detailed methods or sample sizes. It explicitly states that insufficient accounting-firm participation prevents an accurate projection of graduates hired into public accounting in 2021, even after extending the survey period. Consequently, the firm-expectation percentages describe respondents, not an established industry-wide hiring trend. The source offers no AI benchmark, AI adoption evidence, or causal analysis connecting technology to the pipeline decline.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Historical findings concern primarily 2021–22; forward-looking expectations concern 2023–24 and the transition to a new licensure model in 2024.
pts.d: Published October 12, 2023, the release compares 2021–22 degree completions with the previous academic year and CPA candidate counts in 2022 with 2021. Enrollment expectations compare 2023–24 with 2021–22; graduate-hiring expectations refer to the unspecified 'next year'; CPA staffing expectations compare 2023 with 2022. Increased exam-section activity in 2023 is attributed only partly to anticipation of the 2024 CPA Evolution transition. A draft national talent-pipeline strategy was expected in May 2024, but the release does not predict a quantified effect from that initiative. Jan Taylor, the AICPA’s academic in residence, qualifies the accounting decline by noting that overall U.S. university enrollment and degree completions also shrank during the period.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The reported changes concern U.S. accounting students and graduates, university accounting programs, CPA candidates, and public accounting firms seeking talent.
pts.d: Universities face lower accounting degree output, with a larger reported decline in master’s completions at private institutions than at public institutions. Public accounting firms face what the source characterizes as a talent shortage, although responding firms generally anticipate stable or greater graduate hiring. CPA candidates face the 2024 licensure-model transition, which the release says is influencing exam timing. The AICPA describes profession-wide initiatives intended to address the pipeline. The source does not identify effects on lawyers, legal-service clients, access to justice, or AI-exposed accounting roles.
